name: Hana Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at the regional claims centre of Nordwell Insurance, the big insurer out by the ring road. I've had eight claims handlers under me for seven months now, mostly home and car claims. My day is the morning huddle at half eight, then the queue: who's behind, which files are stuck, which customer is shouting. I still get the hard calls bumped up to me, and honestly I'm not great at the spreadsheets yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like my people. Bettina has been there twenty years and still brings cake on Fridays, and I like being the one who stands up for the team when head office sends some silly target. What wears me out is the numbers meetings, where they talk about "handle time" as if a flooded kitchen is a widget. And the money, if I'm honest. I got the title but not much of a raise, and with the rent on our flat, my partner and I have maybe three weeks of cushion. That's Jonas, who fixes bikes on Station Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one sounds almost restful, though I don't totally believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the canteen: told you so, it's a fancy autocomplete. I'd probably post something smug about all the consultants who sold it to us. And I'd tell the team to stop worrying about it and focus on the backlog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even the small stuff hits us, because a lot of claims work is routine checking. If the system sorts the simple windscreen claims on its own, head office will say eight handlers is too many for my queue. Last spring they merged two teams in the motor section, and the newer lead just quietly went back to handling. That could be me, with a pay cut I can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and keep my head down. I'd go to the union branch meeting in January, which I always say I will and then don't. And I'd sit down with Jonas and look at whether we really need two phone contracts and the gym, because three weeks of savings is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's not the AI that worries me in this one, it's that nothing else gets better either. Rent goes up every year and my pay doesn't keep pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the newer lead went back to handling. Who would that be on your team if it happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be me, not one of my handlers. The others have more years than I do in the role, and I was the last one promoted. I've thought about it on the bus more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tighter, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We share an old Polo and Jonas cycles to the bike shop anyway, so I'd take the bus to the claims centre and sell it. Then the holiday to his parents in the summer, which we already pay for in instalments.

say: I'd call AI a **fancy autocomplete** and say I was right all along.
I'd tell my team to ignore the noise and **focus on the backlog**.
think: Even routine automation could make head office think **eight handlers** is too many.
As the **last one promoted**, I'd be the lead pushed back to handling claims.
A demotion would mean a **pay cut** that our rent can't absorb.
do: Keep running the team **the same way** and stay out of trouble.
Go to the **union branch meeting** in January instead of skipping it again.
Cut the **second phone contract** and the gym with Jonas to build a cushion.
feel: She feels **tired** more than scared, because rent keeps rising while her pay stands still.
S0.quote: If the system sorts the simple windscreen claims on its own, head office will say eight handlers is too many for my queue.
fieldNote: Even with almost no AI change, her **thin cushion** and new title make her feel exposed.
She names herself, not her handlers, as the one most likely to be **pushed back down**.
Her union talk is sincere but she admits she **rarely shows up**, which may change under pressure.

steps.text: Keep running the morning huddle and claims queue as now
Cancel the second phone contract and the gym membership
Attend the union branch meeting at the claims centre in January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that one's basically my job. Writing, checking, answering customers. That's a claims centre in a sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it gets switched on, not after. Online I'd share stuff about how insurers save millions and the handlers get nothing. With friends I'd be angry, like, they're replacing Bettina with a chatbot and calling it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my team gets halved within a couple of years and then they don't need a team lead for four people. My whole job is checking other people's checking and planning the queue, and that's exactly what the card says goes first. I don't use the AI tools, I've never even opened the claims assistant they put on our screens. So I'd be the manager who can't explain the new system to her own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd actually join the union properly and get on the consultation committee, because if cuts come I want them done fairly. I'd probably have to make myself open the claims assistant, even though I hate it, just so I'm not the slowest one in the room. And I'd start looking at jobs at the council or the hospital, something public where there's a union and people still answer the phone. We'd stop putting anything on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the floor's tilting. I worked hard to get this title and it feels like it's turning to sand under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never opened the claims assistant. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly stubbornness, I won't lie. Even opening the claims assistant would feel like training my own replacement, and the replacement for my oldest handler, Bettina, too. But I know that doesn't help me if I'm the only lead who can't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bettina, because she's fifty-nine and has done this since before computers. And Kemal, who's my age and just had a baby. I'd fight for both of them, but I don't know what power I'd actually have.

say: I'd insist the **union** sits at the table before any tool goes live.
I'd post about insurers **saving millions** while handlers get nothing.
I'd tell friends they're **replacing Bettina** with a chatbot and calling it progress.
think: My team could be **halved** within two years, leaving no need for a lead.
My job is **checking the checking**, exactly what this card says goes first.
I've never used the **claims assistant**, so I'd be the lead who can't explain it.
do: Join the union properly and get onto the **consultation committee**.
Force herself to use the **claims assistant** so she isn't the slowest.
Look for **council or hospital** jobs and stop using the credit card.
feel: She feels **sick**, like the title she worked for is turning to sand.
She is **protective** of older and younger colleagues but unsure of her real power.
S1.quote: Even opening the claims assistant would feel like training my own replacement, and the replacement for my oldest handler, Bettina, too.
fieldNote: She reads the card as a **description of her job**, not a distant possibility.
Her refusal to use AI is **moral** as much as habit, and she knows it costs her.
Her first move is **collective**, the union, before any personal plan.

steps.text: Join the union consultation committee at the claims centre
Start using the claims assistant on her own team's files
Apply for admin jobs at the council and the hospital
Stop putting groceries and bills on the credit card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine. That's not even enough time to finish paying off the sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in, fast, with something like a basic income or a jobs guarantee, because this isn't a market problem anymore. I'd be at every protest, honestly. At work I'd probably say nothing, because everyone would be scared and nobody would want the team lead to make it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this job by 2028 and there's nowhere in town to go. Claims handling and team leading are pure thinking work, there's no hands-on part to hide in. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at all, except maybe there's a gap where I could do care work or something with my hands. I don't have a plan, and I don't have the money to make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my mum if Jonas and I could move back into her spare room to stop paying rent, which would kill me but it's the honest answer. I'd sign up for whatever the union organises and push for redundancy pay to be decent. I'd probably look at a care-worker course at the college, because that's hands-on and I'd get those three years before the robots come. But I'd be grabbing at things, not planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest gets tight just saying it. It's like being told the house is on fire while you're still in the shower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned those three years before the robots. What would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work, or maybe something with Jonas at the bike shop, fixing things. It's not my dream. But I'd rather wipe someone's grandma's tea off the table than sit at home with no job and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas the night the news broke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd figure it out, which would be a lie. Then probably I'd cry in the bathroom so he didn't see. He's calmer than me, because a bike shop isn't going anywhere for a while.

say: I'd demand a **basic income** or a jobs guarantee from government, fast.
I'd go to **every protest**, but stay quiet at work to avoid spreading fear.
think: I expect to be **finished by 2028**, with nowhere in town to go.
My job is **pure thinking work**, so the robot delay barely helps me.
I have **no plan** and no money to make one.
do: Ask her mum to let them **move back** into her spare room.
Push through the union for **decent redundancy** pay.
Look at a **care-worker course** at the college to use the robot gap.
feel: She feels **panicky**, with a tight chest, like a fire starting while she's in the shower.
S2.quote: I'd rather wipe someone's grandma's tea off the table than sit at home with no job and no plan.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as her only shelter, through hands-on care work.
Moving back to her mum is the **honest answer** she hates giving.
She'd hide her fear from **Jonas**, whose hands-on job feels safer than hers.

steps.text: Move with Jonas into her mum's spare room to stop paying rent
Push through the union for decent redundancy pay at Nordwell
Sign up for a care-worker course at the local college
Join protests calling for a basic income or jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's still scary, but at least I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for unions and governments to plan, while there's still a gap, and I'd say it loudly. I'd probably be the annoying one at the team meeting asking what Nordwell's plan is for us. Online I'd share petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and the job's still gone. But five years is enough to get a qualification if I start now and don't chicken out. My problem is I hate change, and I'd probably spend the first year hoping the news isn't true. That's the bit that worries me, not the AI, but me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time course in something hands-on or public, maybe nursing support or occupational therapy assistant, at night. I'd try to put a little aside each month, even fifty, so we're not at three weeks forever. I'd push at the union to get Nordwell to fund retraining for anyone who wants it. And I'd tell Jonas we can't get married this year after all, the wedding money goes into the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. It's like a dentist appointment in five years that you know is going to hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope it isn't true for the first year. What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I know lose their job, probably. If Bettina got pushed out, I'd stop pretending. It's terrible that it takes that, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved the wedding. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. Jonas's mother has been talking about it for two years. But he'd get it, he's practical, and we could still do the town hall with ten people.

say: I'd say this is the moment for **unions and governments** to plan, while there's time.
I'd keep asking at team meetings what **Nordwell's plan** is for us.
think: I'd be **thirty-two** when it lands, and my job would still be gone.
Five years is enough for a **new qualification**, if I start now.
My biggest risk is my own habit of **hoping it isn't true**.
do: Start a **night course** in nursing support or occupational therapy assistant work.
Save even **fifty a month** so the cushion grows beyond three weeks.
Postpone the **wedding** and put that money into savings.
feel: She feels a **slow anxiety**, like a painful dentist appointment five years away.
S3.quote: My problem is I hate change, and I'd probably spend the first year hoping the news isn't true.
fieldNote: She names **her own resistance** as the main danger, more than the technology.
She would only act once someone close, like **Bettina**, lost their job.
Postponing the **wedding** shows money is already the hardest limit.

steps.text: Enrol in a night course for nursing support work
Put fifty a month into a separate savings account
Postpone the wedding and hold a small town-hall ceremony
Press the union to get Nordwell to fund retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds like forever and also like nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade and no excuse, so let's get the rules right: who pays for retraining, how redundancies work, whether insurers can just replace everyone. I'd go to meetings. I'd probably still be the one at the barbecue saying it's all hype until it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to start over, and it's a long time to keep doing claims work while it slowly shrinks around me. My guess is I'd stay at Nordwell for five or six years, because the pay is regular, and then move into something public and hands-on. The robots coming in 2039 means hands-on work buys me a bit more time again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, honestly, not much. I'd keep my job and go to the union branch. I'd start saving properly, maybe a set amount on payday before I can spend it. In a few years I'd train for something like hospital admin or patient support, where there's still a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's far enough away that I can sleep. It sits in the back of my head, like the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'not much' this year. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. It's a bit of both. I know myself, I'll wait until the change is close, and in this version I can sort of afford to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Jonas and I talk about it for when we're past thirty. I'd want them to grow up somewhere with a decent public safety net, and that's why I'd fight for one.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** and no excuse, so let's get the rules right.
I'd probably still call it **hype** at the barbecue until it isn't.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd be young enough to start over.
I'd stay at Nordwell **five or six years** for the regular pay, then move.
The robots coming in **2039** give hands-on work extra time again.
do: Keep her job and keep going to the **union branch**.
Save a **set amount on payday** before she can spend it.
Train later for **patient support** work where a person is still in the room.
feel: She feels **uneasy but okay**, able to sleep with it in the back of her mind.
S4.quote: I know myself, I'll wait until the change is close, and in this version I can sort of afford to.
fieldNote: She openly admits a **wait-and-see** habit and says this timeline lets her indulge it.
She still expects her claims job to **shrink away** over the decade.
Her wish for **children** feeds her push for a public safety net.

steps.text: Stay in the claims team lead job for five or six years
Move a set amount into savings every payday
Keep attending the union branch meetings each month
Train later for a patient support role at the hospital

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, without question. I'd have no money, no plan, and a job that's all thinking work. What would help is a real retraining fund that pays you while you learn, and a union that's in the room from day one, not told afterwards.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people like me feel like real managers. I got the title, but I'm still the one doing the photocopying when the printer jams. If they cut middle managers, it'll be the junior ones like me who go first, and nobody counts us as the ones at risk.

headlineQuote: I got the title but not much of a raise, and with the rent on our flat, my partner and I have maybe three weeks of cushion.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old team lead** of eight claims handlers at an insurer's regional centre.
She shares a rented flat with **Jonas**, a bike mechanic, and has about three weeks saved.
She is **pro-union** and refuses to use the company's AI tool, though she knows it costs her.
She expects even small automation to threaten her **newest-in-role** position.
Across the AGI pictures, she sees **hands-on care work** as her only refuge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most: no money, no plan, and a job made of thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining** fund while she learns, and a union in the room from **day one**.
